paragraphs.source_en: The eighteenth year of Keichō was drawing to a close, yet the turmoil stirred up by Ōkubo Nagayasu continued to send fearful ripples through the realm, casting a dark cloud of dread not only over the Sanada but over most of the outside lords as well. Tokugawa Ieyasu had left Edo, but instead of returning to Sunpu, he had moved from Nakahara in Musashi to the Kosugi teahouse, where he was said to be staying. This unexpected halt along the way only heightened the lords’ unease and speculation.

paragraphs.source_en: When Tadachika left Odawara Castle, he already had a faint inkling of this punishment. That was the chief reason he had tried to keep Ieyasu forcibly in the castle and remonstrate with him directly. The times had changed. This was no longer the age when lord and retainers shared hardship together in Mikawa, and retainers were no longer permitted to act as they pleased. Perhaps it was in consideration of his ancestors’ devoted service that Ieyasu spared Tadachika’s life. Yet whenever Matsukura Shigemasa recalled the righteous indignation of the honest and loyal Tadachika upon hearing his sentence from the shoshidai, his heart grew heavy.
